what: A wide-column store like Cassandra or ScyllaDB spreads rows across many equal nodes by hashing a partition key. It takes huge write volumes, keeps copies on several nodes and lets you pick consistency per query.
like: Like a giant post office: the postcode (partition key) picks the sorting room, and inside, letters are filed in date order (clustering columns).
why: Writes are very fast: append to a log, update memory, done
No single leader, so any node can serve and you add nodes to grow
Copies across racks and data centres keep it running through failures

steps.d: Any node can act as coordinator. It hashes the partition key to a token on the ring, and the nodes owning that token range hold the data. Vnodes give each node several small ranges.
The write goes to all RF (replication factor) replicas. The coordinator replies once W of them confirm, where W comes from your consistency level: ONE, QUORUM or ALL.
Each replica appends the write to its commit log for durability, then updates the memtable, a sorted in-memory table. No read before write, which is why writes are so quick.
When the memtable fills up it is flushed to disk as an SSTable, a sorted file that is never changed again. This is the LSM tree (log-structured merge tree) pattern.
In the background, compaction merges SSTables, keeps the newest value per cell and drops deleted data once its tombstone (delete marker) is old enough.
A read checks the memtable and SSTables (Bloom filters skip files) on R replicas. If R + W > RF, the read and write sets overlap, so you see the latest acknowledged write.

choices.d: The most important choice. Pick a key that spreads load evenly and lets each query read one partition, for example (user_id, month) for a timeline.
They sort rows inside a partition, such as by time descending, so "latest 20 messages" is one quick slice read.
Use NetworkTopologyStrategy in production and set RF per data centre, commonly 3, so one node can be down while QUORUM still works.
Set per query. LOCAL_QUORUM for reads and writes gives R + W > RF inside one data centre; ONE is fastest but may read slightly stale data.
Size-tiered is the default and suits write-heavy tables. Pick per table to match how data is written, read and expired.

Same partition-key model, fully managed with no nodes to run
When you need an ordered, replayable stream rather than queryable rows
Ad-hoc analytics and big scans across all the data

breaks.d: One partition key gets most of the traffic, so its few replica nodes work flat out.
breaks.see: A few nodes with high CPU and latency while others are calm
breaks.fix: Add a bucket to the key, e.g. (sensor_id, day), to spread load

breaks.d: An unbounded partition keeps growing, making reads, repairs and compaction heavy.
breaks.see: Large-partition warnings in logs, slow reads for one key
breaks.fix: Bound partitions by time or bucket; aim under 100 MB

breaks.d: Many deletes or TTLs leave delete markers that reads must skip over until compaction purges them.
breaks.see: Tombstone warnings in logs, slow range reads
breaks.fix: Model to avoid mass deletes; use TTLs with time-window tables

breaks.d: A replica missed a delete and was not repaired before the tombstone was purged.
breaks.see: Old rows reappear after a node rejoins
breaks.fix: Run full repair at least once within every gc_grace_seconds window

breaks.d: A query does not use the partition key, so it would touch every node.
breaks.see: ALLOW FILTERING in queries, timeouts on reads
breaks.fix: Add a new table shaped for that query and write to both

say: I'll use Cassandra for this write-heavy data, modelled query-first: one table per access pattern, each read hitting one partition.
The partition key is (user_id, month) so partitions stay bounded, and a clustering column sorts by time so the newest rows come first.
With RF 3 and LOCAL_QUORUM on both reads and writes, R + W > RF, so reads see the latest write and one node can be down.
There are no joins, so I denormalise and write the same data to a second table when another query needs it.

followups.q: How does Cassandra decide which node holds a row?
followups.a: It hashes the partition key to a token on a ring. Each node owns token ranges (vnodes), and the replication strategy walks the ring to pick RF replicas, spread across racks and data centres.
It is an LSM tree: a write is a commit log append plus an in-memory memtable update, with no read first. Memtables flush to immutable SSTables, and compaction merges them later.

followups.q: How do replicas that missed writes catch up?
followups.a: Hinted handoff replays writes when a node returns, read repair fixes mismatches seen during reads, and anti-entropy repair compares Merkle trees to sync everything.

followups.q: How do you model a chat app?
followups.a: Start from the query, e.g. "latest messages in a room". Table keyed by (room_id, bucket) with message time as a descending clustering column. Each page of messages is one partition slice.

today: ScyllaDB is a C++ rewrite that speaks Cassandra's CQL (and the DynamoDB API), uses a shard-per-core design, and splits data into same-size tablets instead of vnodes.

check.q: RF is 3. Which consistency levels for reads and writes guarantee you read the latest write?
check.why: 2 + 2 > 3, so read and write replicas always overlap by at least one node.

check.q: Where does a write go first on a replica?
check.a: The commit log, then the memtable
d: A B-tree page updated in place
Only to memory, nothing on disk
check.why: The log gives durability and the memtable keeps data sorted until it is flushed to an SSTable.

check.q: One device sends far more data than all the others and its nodes are overloaded. What is this?
check.why: One partition key lives on a few replicas. Adding a bucket to the key spreads it out.

check.q: What is the first step in Cassandra data modelling?
check.a: List the queries the app will run
check.why: Modelling is query-driven: each table is shaped so one query reads as few partitions as possible.
